key_terms.meaning: A fixed identifiable lump of matter; the Reynolds transport theorem relates what happens to it to what happens in a control volume.
A chosen region in space through which fluid flows; its boundary is the control surface.
The closed boundary of the control volume, area A, through which mass and momentum cross.
A property that scales with the amount of matter, such as mass m, momentum mV or energy E.
An extensive property per unit mass, written with small letters: momentum per unit mass is velocity V, energy per unit mass is e.
The rate at which an intensive property is carried across the control surface: ∫ ρ b (V·n) dA, with n the outward unit normal.
d/dt(B_system) = ∂/∂t ∫_CV ρ b dV + ∫_CS ρ b (V·n) dA; storage term plus net outflux equals the system rate of change.
A curve everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity field; no flow crosses it in steady flow.
Along a streamline of inviscid flow: (1/ρ) dp/ds + g dz/ds + V dV/ds = 0, with s the distance along the streamline.
p/ρg + z + V²/2g = constant along a streamline for steady, incompressible, frictionless flow; the three terms are pressure, elevation and velocity head, each in metres.
The pressure p₀ reached when the flow is brought to rest isentropically: p₀ = p + ρV²/2 for incompressible flow.
A converging–throat–diverging tube; discharge Q = Cd A₂ √(2gH / (1 − (A₂/A₁)²)), where H is the equivalent head difference and A₂ is the throat area.
A thin flat plate with a central hole in a pipe; same equation form as the venturimeter but the vena-contracta area is used.
A tube facing the flow that brings fluid to rest and measures stagnation pressure, giving V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ).
Cd = actual discharge ÷ ideal discharge; it lumps all losses and non-uniformity into one measured number.
Cc = area of jet ÷ area of hole, Cv = actual velocity ÷ ideal velocity, and Cd = Cc × Cv.
Torque on the control volume T = ∫_CS (r × V) ρ (V·n) dA + Σ(r × F_pressure); the moment arm r converts the momentum flux into torque.
ρ DV/Dt = −∇p + ρg + μ∇²V; Newton's second law per unit volume with the viscous shear term included for a Newtonian fluid.
M = V/c, the flow speed divided by the local speed of sound c = √(γRT); above about 0.3 density changes can no longer be ignored.

takeaways: The Reynolds transport theorem is the single machine that converts every law written for a moving lump of fluid into a law usable on a fixed region in space.
Euler's equation is just Newton's second law written along a streamline, and Bernoulli's equation is its integral when density is constant.
Pressure head, elevation head and velocity head are all lengths in metres, so Bernoulli is a statement about a total head that stays constant.
A venturimeter, an orificemeter and a pitot tube are the same idea: one measured pressure difference, one known area, one discharge or velocity.
Every real flow device is handled by adding a single measured coefficient (Cd, Cc, Cv) to the ideal Bernoulli result.
The momentum equation answers force questions that Bernoulli cannot: it survives losses, so it is the tool for bends, vanes and nozzles.
The Navier–Stokes equations are solved exactly only after deleting the terms that vanish by the geometry of the problem, as in plane Poiseuille flow.
Above M ≈ 0.3 the density of a gas changes across a device and the incompressible relations must be replaced by Mach-number relations in γ.
bank_note: Long answers are almost always a derivation plus one numerical case: the standard pattern is to derive the equation from first principles on a small element or control volume, state the assumptions, and then apply it to a venturimeter, notch or pipe bend.

bank.q: State the Reynolds transport theorem for a fixed control volume and explain each term. Show how it reduces to the continuity equation and to the steady-flow energy equation.
outline: Write d/dt∫_sys ρb dV = ∂/∂t∫_CV ρb dV + ∫_CS ρb(V·n)dA
Define system, control volume, control surface, extensive and intensive property
Choose b = 1 for continuity, b = V for momentum, b = e for energy
Show steady flow removes the storage term
State that the theorem holds for any control volume, fixed or moving

bank.q: Derive Euler's equation of motion along a streamline for an inviscid fluid, stating all assumptions, and integrate it to obtain Bernoulli's equation.
outline: Take a cylindrical element of length ds and area dA along the streamline
Forces: pressure on the two faces, weight component ρg dA ds cos θ
Write net force equals mass times acceleration V dV/ds
Obtain dp/ρ + g dz + V dV = 0
Integrate for constant ρ to get p/ρg + z + V²/2g = constant
Assumptions: inviscid, steady, incompressible, along a streamline

bank.q: State Bernoulli's equation and explain the physical meaning of each head. List the assumptions and give two situations in which it fails.
outline: Write the equation with units of metres
Pressure head p/ρg, elevation head z, velocity head V²/2g, total head H
Assumptions: steady, incompressible, frictionless, along a streamline, no shaft work
Failures: viscous pipe flow with friction loss, compressible gas flow above M ≈ 0.3

bank.q: Compare the venturimeter, the orificemeter and the pitot tube: construction, the pressure difference each measures, the equation used, and the relative permanent head loss.
outline: Venturimeter: gradual contraction and diffuser, low loss, area ratio known from throat
Orificemeter: thin plate, vena contracta, high permanent loss, cheap
Pitot tube: single point velocity, stagnation versus static pressure
All three rest on Bernoulli plus continuity
Typical Cd values: about 0.98 venturimeter, 0.6 orificemeter

bank.q: Define the coefficients of contraction, velocity and discharge for a small orifice and derive the relation between them. Distinguish between a notch and a weir.
outline: Cc = a/A, Cv = V_actual/√(2gh), Cd = Q_actual/Q_ideal
Derive Cd = Cc × Cv
Notch: opening with the liquid surface as its upper edge; weir: notch in a channel wall, usually larger
Name the types: rectangular, triangular, trapezoidal
Mention the velocity of approach and why it raises the discharge

bank.q: A venturimeter with pipe diameter 200 mm and throat diameter 100 mm carries oil of relative density 0.85. A mercury manometer reads 150 mm. Taking Cd = 0.98, find the discharge in litres per second.
outline: Convert the manometer reading to oil head: H = x(SG_Hg/SG_oil − 1)
Area ratio A₂/A₁ = (100/200)² = 0.25
Apply Q = Cd A₂ √(2gH/(1 − (A₂/A₁)²))
State the answer with units, in L/s
Comment on the loss between inlet and throat

bank.q: A pitot-static tube is placed in an air stream at 30 °C where the static pressure is 101 kPa. The stagnation pressure measured is 102.2 kPa. Find the air velocity, stating the assumption about density.
outline: Use p₀ = p + ρV²/2 for incompressible flow
Compute ρ = p/RT with R = 287 J/(kg·K)
Solve V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ)
Check the Mach number to confirm M < 0.3
Give V in m/s and note the pitot coefficient if the tube is not ideal

bank.q: Water flows over a rectangular notch 1.2 m wide under a head of 0.25 m with Cd = 0.62. Find the discharge. Include the velocity of approach and state how much the discharge changes compared with neglecting it.
outline: Compute the base value with H only
Velocity of approach Va = Q/(b(H + y)) for the channel
Replace H by the total head H + Va²/2g
Compare the two answers and state the percentage rise

bank.q: Water flows at 0.05 m³/s through a horizontal 90° reducing bend from 150 mm to 100 mm diameter. The pressure at inlet is 150 kPa. Using the momentum equation, find the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the bend on the water.
outline: Use continuity to get both velocities
Use Bernoulli to get the outlet pressure
Apply the linear momentum equation in both x and y directions
Include the pressure force terms pA on each face
Resultant force R = √(Fx² + Fy²) and angle tan θ = Fy/Fx
State clearly that the force by the fluid on the bend is equal and opposite

bank.q: A large tank holds water 3 m above a small sharp-edged orifice of 50 mm diameter with Cd = 0.62. Find the initial discharge and the time for the level to fall to 1 m in a tank of 2 m² plan area.
outline: Q = Cd A √(2gh) for the initial head
For falling head: dt = −A_tank dh/(Cd A √(2gh))
Integrate from h₁ to h₂
t = (2A_tank/(Cd A √(2g)))(√h₁ − √h₂)
Give both answers with units

bank.q: Starting from the Navier–Stokes equations, obtain the velocity profile for steady fully developed laminar flow between two infinite parallel plates at distance 2h apart, driven by a pressure gradient, and find the discharge per unit width.
outline: Set v = w = 0, u = u(y) only
Convective and unsteady terms vanish; reduce to 0 = −dp/dx + μ d²u/dy²
Integrate twice with u = 0 at y = ±h
Obtain u = (1/2μ)(−dp/dx)(h² − y²)
Integrate over the section for discharge per unit width
Note the maximum velocity at the centreline

bank.q: Starting from the Reynolds transport theorem, derive the linear momentum equation for a control volume and use it to obtain the force on a pipe bend. Explain why the pressure forces on the control surface must be included while the Bernoulli approach alone cannot give the force.
outline: Set b = V in the transport theorem
For steady flow Σ F = ∫_CS V ρ(V·n)dA, an outflux minus an influx
Σ F includes pressure forces, weight and the reaction from the bend
Show the sign convention for the outward normal
Explain that momentum is a vector balance and is unaffected by friction losses, unlike Bernoulli
Note that in an accelerating control volume an extra inertia term appears

bank.q: Examine the assumptions behind Bernoulli's equation and judge, with an example in each case, how the equation fails for a viscous oil pipeline, a pump, and an air flow at M = 0.6.
outline: List the four assumptions and the meaning of each
Viscous pipe: add the friction head loss hf; Bernoulli becomes an energy balance with loss
Pump: add shaft work head; sign convention for work done on the fluid
Compressible: density changes, use p₀/p = (1 + (γ−1)M²/2)^(γ/(γ−1))
State the M ≈ 0.3 threshold and roughly 5 per cent density error
Conclude that Bernoulli is a special case of the energy equation

bank.q: Choose a flow meter for measuring the water supply to a large housing society, comparing venturimeter, orificemeter and ultrasonic options on head loss, accuracy, cost and maintenance, and justify your choice.
outline: State the duty: pipe size, expected flow range, allowable head loss
Venturimeter: low permanent loss, high cost, well-proven
Orificemeter: cheap, high permanent loss, poor at low flow
Rota/ultrasonic: no obstruction, higher cost, needs power
Estimate annual energy cost of the head loss for one choice
Justify with the numbers, not adjectives

glossary.def: Mass is conserved: for steady flow through a stream tube, ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂, and Q = AV for an incompressible fluid.
The imaginary closed boundary that separates the chosen control volume from its surroundings.
A fixed region of space chosen for analysis, through which fluid may flow.
Coefficient of discharge, the ratio of actual to ideal discharge, always less than 1.
Coefficient of contraction, the ratio of the vena-contracta area to the orifice area.
Coefficient of velocity, the ratio of the actual jet velocity to the ideal √(2gh).
Describing a flow by the velocity and pressure fields at fixed points in space, rather than by following individual particles.
Energy per unit weight of fluid, expressed as a length in metres; for example V²/2g is the velocity head.
The line joining the piezometric heads p/ρg + z along a pipe, ignoring the velocity head.
The ratio of flow speed to local speed of sound, M = V/√(γRT).
The rate at which momentum crosses a surface, equal to ρAV² for uniform flow through area A at velocity V.
A short tube fitted to an orifice that changes the coefficient of discharge by controlling the vena contracta.
The momentum equations for a Newtonian fluid, containing the viscous term μ∇²V.
An opening in a tank or channel wall with the free liquid surface as its upper edge, used to measure discharge in open channels.
A small opening, usually in the base or side of a tank, through which fluid discharges and forms a jet.
The sum p/ρg + z at a point, measured by a piezometer tapping.
A bent tube with an open end facing the flow that measures stagnation pressure and hence local velocity.
The identity that equates the rate of change of a property of a system to the storage rate inside a control volume plus the net flux out of it.
A point in the flow where the velocity is zero and the pressure is the stagnation pressure.
A scalar ψ whose derivatives give the velocity components in two-dimensional incompressible flow, so that ψ = constant along a streamline.
The sum p/ρg + z + V²/2g, constant along a streamline in ideal steady flow.
The smallest cross-section of a jet just downstream of an orifice, where the streamlines become parallel again.
A converging–throat–diverging meter that measures pipe discharge from the pressure difference between the inlet and the throat.
The small velocity of the liquid surface in the channel feeding a notch; its head Va²/2g is added to the measured head.
A notch built across an open channel, usually rectangular or triangular, over which the water spills.
The line integral of velocity around a closed curve, Γ = ∮V·ds; it is zero in irrotational flow.
